title: India's sugar prices hold near record highs as festive demand mounts
excerpt: Retail sugar touched ₹85/kg in some markets as weak rains and disease cut production, forcing duty-free imports and stock limits weeks before Diwali.
body:
• Retail sugar averaged ₹59.57/kg across India on September 14, with prices touching ₹85/kg in some markets — roughly double what they were in parts of the country a year ago.
  • Production for the 2025-26 season is now estimated at 30.6 million tonnes, 11% below the government's earlier forecast, after patchy rains, crop disease and farmers shifting away from cane.
  • New Delhi has allowed 1 million tonnes of duty-free imports through October 31, capped stockholding and warned mills against price hikes — but prices remain nearly 20% above where they were two months ago.
  • The squeeze lands hardest on low-income households and sweet-makers: India's $1.1-billion sweets trade earns more than 40% of its annual revenue during the festive season.

A festive season with less sugar in it

With Diwali less than two months away, India's sweetest season is turning bitter. The average all-India retail price of sugar stood at ₹59.57 per kg on Monday, according to Consumer Affairs Ministry data — down from its record highs last month but still elevated despite a string of government interventions. Prices have remained above the ₹58.23/kg recorded on August 21, when New Delhi first allowed duty-free imports, and in some markets they have touched ₹85/kg. The minimum, in others, is ₹40.

The government says India has adequate stocks. It has accused mills and traders of hoarding in anticipation of festive-season demand and has warned it will take corrective action to keep prices stable. "It is the collective responsibility of the entire sector to ensure that prices remain stable. There is no justification for any price rise during festivals," Ashwini Srivastava, a joint secretary in the food ministry, said earlier this month.

But for Jai Krishan, a 43-year-old labourer from Bihar working in Kashmir, the numbers translate into a simpler arithmetic. He has saved ₹15,000 to travel home for Diwali in November and usually spends about $35 on boxes of laddu, barfi and kaju katli for his family. This year, with sugar nearly doubling in some markets from ₹40 a year ago, he has started walking eight kilometres to work to save ₹50 a day on transport. "What difference does it make to the rich? They will celebrate the festival with great pomp and show anyway. It is poor people like me who will bear the impact," he said.

Why sugar is so expensive this year

India is the world's largest consumer of sugar and its second-largest producer, usually making enough for its needs with some left over to export. Not this year. Government data puts 2025-26 production at about 30.6 million tonnes — 11% below the earlier estimate of 34.3 million tonnes. Annual domestic demand is pegged at 280-285 lakh tonnes, and analyst firm ICRA estimates inventories will fall to 4.3 million tonnes by September, leaving less than two months of consumption cover ahead of the festival rush.

The government blames lower sugarcane cultivation, patchy rainfall during El Niño conditions and hoarding. Farmers point to a longer list. Sugarcane growers in Punjab and Uttar Pradesh say returns no longer cover costs: one Punjab farmer estimates producing 100 kg of sugar costs ₹470 once labour, irrigation, cultivation and transport are counted, against returns of only ₹416 — a loss of ₹54 per 100 kg. High labour costs, soil degradation, delayed payments from mills and vulnerability of the dominant Co-0238 cane variety to red rot disease have pushed some farmers toward other crops.

Ethanol diversion is contested. The government says the share of sugar diverted to ethanol has fallen from about 12% in 2022-23 to about 9% in 2025-26, with nearly three-quarters of India's ethanol now made from grains such as maize. Farmers, and industry analysts, are less sure the blending programme is innocent. Meanwhile, higher fuel costs linked to the US-Israel war on Iran have raised irrigation pumping costs, adding to growers' expenses.

Sweet-makers, households and packaged-food companies feel the pinch

Sweets are inseparable from the season: India's sweets sector is worth more than $1.1 billion, with festive sales accounting for over 40% of annual revenue, and traditional mithai can be 30 to 60% sugar by weight. Patna resident Aman Jaswal said sweets are costing 15 to 20% more this year. "Sweets are closely tied to happiness in Indian culture," he said. "Gifting sweets is a way of sharing happiness and it has become part of our celebrations and relationships."

The pressure extends to factory gates. Rising sugar prices are expected to compress gross margins of packaged-food companies by 50-80 basis points in the September quarter, according to Saurav Chaube, an equity research analyst at Samco Securities, with companies having limited room to pass costs on to consumers who have already absorbed higher prices across milk-based drinks, chocolates and biscuits.

"The measure is best understood as a price ceiling rather than a price cut. That price now limits how high domestic sugar can go, because once imported sugar is cheaper, no mill can hold its own price above the landed cost for long."

— Sanjay Kumar, professor of economics at Delhi University

Kumar was describing the government's duty-free import window, under which sugar can be landed at about $0.55 per kg. But he notes the ceiling has not held so far — the imports are raw sugar, while Indian demand is mainly for refined.

Diaspora angle

For diaspora households preparing for Diwali abroad, the pinch travels along the supply chain: gift parcels of mithai sent home cost more this year, and Indian grocery stores and halwai shelves overseas that price festive sweets off Indian wholesale markets are likely to reflect the surge.

What's next

New Delhi has authorised the duty-free import of 1 million tonnes of raw sugar until October 31, and says applications for 800,000 tonnes have already come in. It has ordered that bulk consumers and dealers using more than 10 tonnes a month hold no more than 15 days of inventory between September 1 and November 30, and will now track sugar production monthly to tighten policymaking.

Industry body ISMA insists there is no structural shortage, estimating closing stocks of around 35 lakh tonnes and expecting prices to ease as fresh-season supplies arrive and the crushing season is advanced. The government is also importing sugar from Brazil for the first time in nearly a decade. Whether those levers cool prices before the Diwali peak — or whether households and sweet-makers face the costliest festive season in years — will become clear in the coming weeks.
